items.title: Doc Cheatham interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, New York City, New York, July 28, 1995
items.q: Well you know I never tried to play that style of music — Buck Clayton, Sweets Edison and the rest of them — because that’s the western band from Bennie Moten’s band.

ctx.x: Well you know I never tried to play that style of music — Buck Clayton, Sweets Edison and the rest of them — because that’s the western band from Bennie Moten’s band. That band started out playing blues, that’s the way it was. Then later on through the years it started swinging, and still with the blues accent. And I was never a blues trumpet player. If I have to play it I’ll play it. But everything they had was swing and jump. And I was offered a job with Basie. He asked me one time he came and heard me play and…

say no one can play like Bird — they are in a class with Louis Armstrong. And you can’t kid yourself you know. I’m not going to jump in a band like that. So the Countsmen were never successful. They had Earle Warren leading and he was taking the lead, and he was leading the band. And he wasn’t in Count Basie’s band as the leader, see? But he couldn’t make it. He’s too loud and he was excited and he got upset all the time at things, and you can’t do that. So I’m just playing and I thank God for whatever I’m able…

items.title: 54270_Doc Cheatham oral history interview
items.q: they sent me to Nancy, to play in Buck's place... we went out there and the opened up and played

ctx.x: -- and I felt absolutely lost, as a soloist because to get up there and play New Orleans style of solo in that band, would be -- have been out of place, entirely out of place and it wouldn't have fitted in there in the first place. It would've been entirely out of place. But you see there were a lot of other trumpet -- but New York you had other trumpet players that, you know, you were listening to at different times, like Buck Clayton.

items.title: 67246_Buck Clayton oral history interview
items.q: [INTERVIEWER] There are people like Doc Cheatham and Money Johnson. ... [INTERVIEWEE] Yes, I know. Yes, it gets scarce.

ctx.x: I know. Snookey is a good man.
There are people like Doc Cheatham and Money Johnson. But there are very few left. Pat Jenkins.

Yes, I know. Yes, it gets scarce. Very scarce. People like Emmett Berry, Charlie Shavers. Some of them it just didn't seem to me that they are still not here. You know, like as healthy as Red Allen was at the Metropole and as good natured, a good kind of guy he was it just doesn't seem like things like that could happen, but they do.
